To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the RhoGTPases RhoA and Rac1 are activated and inhibited in a coordinated, periodic fashion at the leading and the trailing edge during cell movement; (2) this coordination is achieved by a network of biochemical interactions between RhoA and its regulators; and (3) this network is sufficient and necessary for the observed coordination of Rho and Rac dynamics at the leading edge and trailing edge during cell migration.
the RhoGTPases RhoA and Rac1 coordinate their activities in a spatially periodic manner during cell migration.
periodic, propagating Rho GTPase waves are sufficient and necessary for the coordination of the GTPase network at the leading and the trailing edge during cell migration.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular mechanism of the cell migration.
the coordination of the dynamics of the Rho GTPases RhoA and Rac1 in the leading and trailing regions of migrating cells.
the mechanisms of cell motility and the role of the Rho family of GTPases in cell movement.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
RhoGTPases are not just a bunch of GTPase molecules, but a network of GTPase proteins that are tightly interconnected and that coordinate their activities to allow cells to move.
the oscillatory dynamics of the GTPases RhoA, Rac1, and Cdc42 is the basis of the periodic, propagating wave of protrusions and retracions that drives cell migration.

RhoA ROCK and RhoA DRA interactions at the rear are necessary and sufficient for cell retraction, while Rac1 RhoA DLA interactions at the front are necessary and sufficient to induce cell protrusion and cell movement.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the periodic propagating waves coordinate the GTPase network dynamics in migrating cells.
the cell front and the cell rear are dynamically coordinated via propagating waves of GTPase activities, which in turn control the cell front and cell rear dynamics.
the periodic propagating GTPASE waves coordinate Rho GTPase network dynamics to drive cell movement.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the cell can coordinate distinct leading and rear edge dynamics by a simple, periodic propagating wave of GTPase activities that is initiated at the leading edge.
the coordination of the RhoA, Rac1, and RhoGDI network is sufficient for cell migration and that the network dynamics is driven by a periodic propagating wave.
the RhoA D/ROCK/PAR6/PAK/Rac1 network can autonomously generate periodic propagating waves of RhoGTPases that drive cell movement.
